title: IELTS Listening: Practice Tests
description: Two full Listening practice tests in the real four-part format, 40 questions each: an everyday conversation, a talk about local services, a discussion between students and a tutor, and a short academic lecture. Read the questions first; the recording plays once, as in the exam, so write while you listen. About 30/40 is often around band 7; this is a rough guide, not official. Written for Bo-ok.

units.title: Test 1 · Part 1: Booking a Holiday Cottage
units.goal: Questions 1–10: form completion from a phone call; a name spelled letter by letter, a date, prices and a self-correction.

blocks.text: You will hear a woman phoning a holiday letting agency to book a cottage. Read the questions first. The recording plays once, as in the exam, with a short pause before questions 6–10.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Test one. Part one. You will hear a woman phoning a holiday letting agency to book a cottage. First, you have some time to look at questions one to five.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions one to five.

lines.speaker: graham
lines.text: Good morning, Brackenfield Holiday Cottages, Graham speaking. How can I help?

lines.speaker: joanna
lines.text: Oh, hello. I'd like to book a cottage for a family holiday in August, if you've still got anything free.

lines.speaker: graham
lines.text: We've got a few left, yes. Can I start with your name?

lines.speaker: joanna
lines.text: Of course. It's Joanna Pendry.

lines.speaker: graham
lines.text: Is that P-E-N-D-R-E-Y?

lines.speaker: joanna
lines.text: No, there's no E near the end. It's P-E-N-D-R-Y. Pendry.

lines.speaker: graham
lines.text: Got it, thanks. And how many of you will there be?

lines.speaker: joanna
lines.text: Four adults and two children. My parents are coming with us this year.

lines.speaker: graham
lines.text: Right, so six people. I was going to suggest Willow Cottage, but that only sleeps four, so that's out. The one that'd suit you best is Heron Cottage. It's got three bedrooms and a big garden at the back.

lines.speaker: joanna
lines.text: Heron, like the bird?

lines.speaker: graham
lines.text: Exactly. H-E-R-O-N. It's right by the stream.

lines.speaker: joanna
lines.text: That sounds lovely. We were hoping to arrive on the thirteenth of August.

lines.speaker: graham
lines.text: Let me just check. Hmm, I'm afraid Heron's booked until the morning of the fourteenth.

lines.speaker: joanna
lines.text: Oh. Well, the fourteenth's fine, actually. That's a Saturday, isn't it? It'll be easier for the drive anyway.

lines.speaker: graham
lines.text: It is a Saturday. So that's arrival on the fourteenth of August. And how long would you like to stay?

lines.speaker: joanna
lines.text: We'd thought about a week, but my husband can only get five days off work, so let's say five nights.

lines.speaker: graham
lines.text: Five nights, lovely. Now, the price. Normally it's a hundred and ten pounds a night, but in August we've got a special rate for stays of five nights or more, so it comes down to ninety-five a night.

lines.speaker: joanna
lines.text: Ninety-five. That's very reasonable.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions six to ten.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions six to ten.

lines.speaker: graham
lines.text: Is there anything else you'll be bringing with you? Some families bring bikes, for example.

lines.speaker: joanna
lines.text: No bikes this time, but we'd like to bring our dog. Is that allowed?

lines.speaker: graham
lines.text: Dogs are welcome at Heron, yes. There's an extra charge of fifteen pounds for a dog. That's for the whole stay, not per night.

lines.speaker: joanna
lines.text: That's fine. And what about shops? I'd rather not drive every time we need milk.

lines.speaker: graham
lines.text: There's a big supermarket in Dunmore, but that's a twenty-minute drive. The nearest shop is in Ashcombe, the next village, about a mile away. That's A-S-H-C-O-M-B-E.

lines.speaker: joanna
lines.text: Ashcombe. OK. And do we need to bring any bedding?

lines.speaker: graham
lines.text: No, the beds are made up for you and bed linen's included. You'll need to bring your own towels, though. We used to supply them, but we stopped last year.

lines.speaker: joanna
lines.text: Towels. I'll make a note of that. And how do we get in when we arrive?

lines.speaker: graham
lines.text: Normally there's a key box by the front door, but it's being replaced at the moment, so this summer you'll need to collect the key from the farmhouse. It's the big white house at the end of the lane, where the owners live.

lines.speaker: joanna
lines.text: The farmhouse, fine. And how much do you need now to confirm the booking?

lines.speaker: graham
lines.text: We ask for a deposit. It's usually a hundred pounds, but for six guests and a dog it's a hundred and fifty pounds. The rest is due four weeks before you arrive.

lines.speaker: joanna
lines.text: OK, a hundred and fifty. Can I pay that by card now?

lines.speaker: graham
lines.text: Of course. I'll just take the details.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: That is the end of Part one.

units.title: Test 1 · Part 2: A Morning at Kestrel Water Country Park
units.goal: Questions 11–20: multiple choice and a map in words, from a ranger's talk; listen for places that have moved.

blocks.text: You will hear a park ranger talking to visitors. Read the questions first. The recording plays once, as in the exam, with a short pause before questions 15–20.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Part two. You will hear a park ranger talking to a group of visitors at Kestrel Water Country Park. First, you have some time to look at questions eleven to fourteen.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions eleven to fourteen.

lines.speaker: liam
lines.text: Morning, everyone, and welcome to Kestrel Water. My name's Liam and I'm one of the rangers here. I'll just give you a quick introduction before you head off and explore.

lines.speaker: liam
lines.text: First, a bit of history. A lot of visitors assume this was always farmland, and there were a couple of farms here a long time ago. But for most of the last century the whole site was a gravel quarry. When the digging stopped in nineteen ninety-four, the pits slowly filled with water, and that's how we got our lakes.

lines.speaker: liam
lines.text: You might also hear people mention the old airfield, but that's a few miles further north, not here.

lines.speaker: liam
lines.text: Now, the visitor centre, which is the building right behind me. It's open every day from nine till five. People often think we close early in winter, but we don't; the hours are the same all year round. It was extended last spring, so there's now a big room for school groups and a little exhibition about the quarry.

lines.speaker: liam
lines.text: One thing to remember: parking isn't free. It's three pounds for the day, and you pay at the machine.

lines.speaker: liam
lines.text: A word about the wildlife. Dogs are welcome on all the paths as long as they're on a lead. What we do ask is that you don't give the ducks and swans bread. It's actually bad for them. If you'd like to feed them, you can buy a bag of bird seed in the centre for a pound.

lines.speaker: liam
lines.text: And if you're keen on birds, come along to our guided walk on Sunday. It used to start at seven, which was a bit early for most people, so now it starts at half past eight. Don't confuse it with the children's pond-dipping session, which is at ten.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions fifteen to twenty.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions fifteen to twenty.

lines.speaker: liam
lines.text: OK, let me tell you where everything is. We're at the main entrance, on the south side of the park.

lines.speaker: liam
lines.text: Let's start with the café. Some of you might remember the old café beside the car park, but that building's used for staff offices now. The new café is just behind the visitor centre, so you'll find it in less than a minute.

lines.speaker: liam
lines.text: Next, the bird hide. You might expect it to be on the island in the middle of the big lake, but the island's closed to visitors to protect the nests. Instead, the hide's at the end of the boardwalk, which goes out over the reed beds on the east side.

lines.speaker: liam
lines.text: If you've brought lunch, the picnic area is up at the top of the park, next to the north lake. There are tables there and plenty of shade.

lines.speaker: liam
lines.text: Families with young children usually want the play area. It was down by the boathouse for years, but we moved it because of the water. It's now near the west gate, well away from the lakes, and it's fenced in.

lines.speaker: liam
lines.text: If anyone feels unwell or has an accident, there's a first aid point. You'll find it opposite the boathouse, in the small green hut. There's always a member of staff there at weekends.

lines.speaker: liam
lines.text: And finally, the sculpture trail. It's about two kilometres long and the start is beside the main car park, so a lot of people walk it at the end of their visit, on the way back to their cars. Right, that's everything. Enjoy your day.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: That is the end of Part two.

units.title: Test 1 · Part 3: Planning a Survey on Student Sleep
units.goal: Questions 21–30: multiple choice and matching opinions in a tutorial; ideas are suggested, then rejected.

blocks.text: You will hear two students and their tutor discussing a research project. Read the questions first. The recording plays once, as in the exam, with a short pause before questions 26–30.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Part three. You will hear two students, Kirsty and Dan, talking to their tutor, Dr Ferris, about a research project on student sleep. First, you have some time to look at questions twenty-one to twenty-five.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions twenty-one to twenty-five.

lines.speaker: ferris
lines.text: Come in, both of you. So, you've chosen sleep for your project. Was that one of the topics on the list I gave out?

lines.speaker: kirsty
lines.text: It wasn't on your list, actually. We picked it because so many people on our course look exhausted in the morning lectures. Half the room is yawning by ten o'clock.

lines.speaker: dan
lines.text: And we did worry a bit, because there's loads written about student sleep already. But we thought we could focus on our own university.

lines.speaker: kirsty
lines.text: We've also got until the end of term, so we thought there'd be enough time to collect some proper data, not just read about it.

lines.speaker: ferris
lines.text: That's fine. A lot of existing research just means you'll have plenty to read. Now, who are you planning to ask?

lines.speaker: dan
lines.text: My idea was to survey people living in the halls of residence, because that's where the noise problems are.

lines.speaker: ferris
lines.text: Hmm, I think that's too narrow. Most second- and third-years live in shared houses in town.

lines.speaker: kirsty
lines.text: First-years only, then? They're the easiest to reach.

lines.speaker: ferris
lines.text: You could, but it'd be far more interesting to compare the years. Do sleep habits change as people go through the course?

lines.speaker: dan
lines.text: OK, that makes sense. So, students from every year of the course, then.

lines.speaker: kirsty
lines.text: Agreed. And for collecting the data, we'd thought about an online questionnaire.

lines.speaker: ferris
lines.text: The trouble with a one-off questionnaire is that people don't really remember how long they slept last Tuesday.

lines.speaker: dan
lines.text: We did think about face-to-face interviews, but they'd take far too long for a project this size.

lines.speaker: kirsty
lines.text: So what about a sleep diary? Each person fills it in every morning for a week.

lines.speaker: ferris
lines.text: That would give you much better data. I'd go with that.

lines.speaker: dan
lines.text: Some people suggested we just use the sleep apps on their phones. They record everything automatically.

lines.speaker: ferris
lines.text: They do, and most of them are free, and they're reasonably accurate for total hours. My worry is privacy. You'd be collecting very personal data from people's phones, and that raises all sorts of questions about who can see it.

lines.speaker: kirsty
lines.text: Fair enough, the diary it is. So, should we start by writing the instructions for it?

lines.speaker: ferris
lines.text: You'll need those, of course. But the very first thing is to try the diary out on three or four friends, as a small pilot. Then fix any problems, and after that send in the ethics form.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions twenty-six to thirty.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions twenty-six to thirty.

lines.speaker: ferris
lines.text: Now, your reading list. You've got five sources here. Let's go through them.

lines.speaker: dan
lines.text: The first is the article by Marlow and Chen. It's got some striking results.

lines.speaker: ferris
lines.text: It has, but look at how many people they studied: only forty students, all at one college. I wouldn't build too much on it.

lines.speaker: kirsty
lines.text: Then there's the national health report.

lines.speaker: ferris
lines.text: That was very thorough in its day, but it's from two thousand and nine, before most students had smartphones in bed with them. A lot has changed since then.

lines.speaker: dan
lines.text: What about Okafor's textbook? It looked a bit scientific when I flicked through it.

lines.speaker: ferris
lines.text: It's not as technical as you'd think. The early chapters explain the basics clearly, and the references will lead you to everything else. I'd read that before anything else.

lines.speaker: kirsty
lines.text: And we found a survey the student union did last year about well-being.

lines.speaker: ferris
lines.text: The results are a bit general, but look at how they worded their questions. They're short and clear. You could borrow some of that style for your own diary.

lines.speaker: dan
lines.text: Last one is a podcast series. It's really entertaining.

lines.speaker: ferris
lines.text: I'm sure it is, but as far as I know the presenters are just sharing their own opinions and experiences. There's no study behind it, so I wouldn't quote it as evidence.

lines.speaker: kirsty
lines.text: OK. Thanks, Dr Ferris, that's really helpful.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: That is the end of Part three.

blocks.text: Questions 21–25. Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

blocks.prompt: 21. Why did the students choose sleep as their topic?
options: They noticed that classmates seemed tired.
Very little has been written about it.

why.tr: Kirsty: "It wasn't on your list ... We picked it because so many people on our course look exhausted." A yanlış: listede değildi. C tersi: "there's loads written about student sleep already".
why.ar: Kirsty: "It wasn't on your list ... so many people on our course look exhausted". A خطأ: لم يكن في القائمة. C عكس ما قيل: "there's loads written".
why.en: "We picked it because so many people on our course look exhausted." It wasn't on the list; there's "loads written".

blocks.example: I chose this topic because so many of my friends seemed stressed.

blocks.prompt: 22. Which students will they include in the study?

lines.text: Part four. You will hear a lecture on how people kept ice before refrigerators. First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.

lines.speaker: lect
lines.text: Good afternoon. Today's lecture is about something we take completely for granted: keeping things cold. Long before the electric fridge, people found ways to store ice through the summer, and the building they used was the ice house.

lines.speaker: lect
lines.text: The idea itself is very old. There are records of ice pits in Persia and China more than two thousand years ago. In Britain, though, ice houses only became fashionable in the seventeenth century, when wealthy landowners copied what they had seen on their travels in Italy and France. By the eighteen hundreds, almost every large country estate had one.

lines.speaker: lect
lines.text: Let's begin with where the ice came from. In northern Europe, it was usually cut by hand in the depths of winter. Some estates had rivers nearby, but river ice was often dirty and broke up quickly in moving water. So most ice was cut from ponds and lakes, where the water was still and the ice grew thick. Some landowners even dug shallow ponds specially for this purpose.

lines.speaker: lect
lines.text: The next challenge was keeping it. The key enemy of stored ice isn't really the warm air; it's water. Once ice starts to melt, the water around it speeds up the melting. That's why an ice house was almost always built on a slope, so that meltwater could drain away downhill through a channel at the bottom.

lines.speaker: lect
lines.text: Most ice houses were partly underground, with a domed roof. The walls were very thick. On some estates in rocky areas you'll find stone, but by far the most common material was brick, often two or three layers of it, with a gap between the layers to hold air.

lines.speaker: lect
lines.text: Inside, the ice was packed in tightly, and every layer was covered with straw, which acted as insulation. In the nineteenth century some owners switched to sawdust, but straw remained the usual choice on country estates because it cost almost nothing.

lines.speaker: lect
lines.text: How well did all this work? Surprisingly well. A small or badly built ice house might be empty by midsummer, but a good one could keep ice for up to two years. Records from one estate show ice cut in one winter still being used the winter after next.

lines.speaker: lect
lines.text: Getting the ice out was a job in itself. A servant would climb down a ladder through a small door, often wearing a thick coat even in August, and break off what was needed with a pick. The door was kept shut as much as possible, because every time it opened, warm air got in.

lines.speaker: lect
lines.text: So what was all this ice used for? You might imagine it was mainly for keeping meat fresh, and it was used that way, but the records tell a different story. Doctors valued it highly. Ice was used to bring down a fever, and this was probably its most important use in the early period.

lines.speaker: lect
lines.text: For wealthy families, of course, ice was also a luxury and a way of showing off. At dinner parties, cooks used it to make sorbet, flavoured with fruit from the estate's own gardens, and guests were expected to be impressed.

lines.speaker: lect
lines.text: In the nineteenth century, things changed dramatically. Home-grown ice was never enough for the growing cities, so ice began to be imported. Huge blocks were shipped across the North Sea from Norway, where the lakes froze hard and the ice was very clean. It was stored in large warehouses near the docks and then delivered to shops and hospitals.

lines.speaker: lect
lines.text: But imported natural ice didn't last long as a business either. By the end of the century, ice could be made artificially, all year round, in factories, using machines that compressed gas. This ice was cheaper and more reliable, and the import trade declined quickly. Then, in the twentieth century, the electric refrigerator brought cold into every kitchen, and the ice houses were simply abandoned.

lines.speaker: lect
lines.text: Many have collapsed, but some survive, and a few have found an unexpected new purpose. Because they're cool, dark and stay at a steady temperature, they make ideal winter homes for bats, and several are now protected for exactly that reason.

lines.speaker: lect
lines.text: Next week we'll look at how refrigeration changed the way cities were fed. Thank you.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: That is the end of Part four.

lines.text: Let me start with a bit of background. A lot of people assume the city council runs the market. lines.speaker: megan
lines.text: It's grown a lot since then. In the first year there were just twelve stalls. This year we're expecting over a hundred, selling everything from cheese and bread to spices and fresh fish, and around fifteen thousand visitors over the weekend.

lines.speaker: megan
lines.text: So what's different this year? Well, the children's area was such a success last year that it's coming back. lines.speaker: lang
lines.text: Thanks for coming in, both of you. I wanted to talk about your presentation on food packaging while it's still fresh.

lines.speaker: rosa
lines.text: We were a bit nervous about it, to be honest.

lines.speaker: lang
lines.text: It didn't show. Your slides were clear, if a little crowded in places. But what really stood out for me was the examples you collected from shops here in town. Bringing in real packets from the high street made it feel very concrete.

lines.text: That was Rosa's idea. She spent a whole Saturday going round the shops.

lines.speaker: rosa
lines.text: It was fun, actually. What about the audience? Did they follow it?

lines.speaker: lang
lines.text: Mostly. Nobody had trouble hearing you, and you finished just under twenty minutes, which was right. The main thing on the feedback forms was that you used terms like compostable and bio-based without explaining them. Several people got lost there.

lines.speaker: tom
lines.text: Fair point. We'd been reading about it for so long that we forgot other people hadn't.

lines.speaker: lang
lines.text: It happens. How did you find the research side, Rosa?

lines.speaker: rosa
lines.text: I thought the survey would be the hard part, but we got plenty of responses in a week. The real problem was the packaging companies. We emailed eleven of them and most never replied, and the two that did wouldn't share any figures.

lines.speaker: tom
lines.text: Which was frustrating, because we wanted to compare what they say on their websites with what actually happens.

lines.speaker: lang
lines.text: That's very common, I'm afraid. Companies are often careful about what they share. You did the right thing by saying so in the presentation. And Tom, you looked less comfortable than Rosa up there. What would you do differently?

lines.text: Shall we rewrite the introduction? I wasn't sure about it.

lines.text: No, honestly, the introduction was spot on. Short, with a clear question. I wouldn't change a word.

lines.speaker: tom
lines.text: What about the history of plastic packaging? I thought that went well.

lines.speaker: lang

lines.speaker: lang
lines.text: Some did, because you made big claims without any evidence. Find some real numbers, like how much it costs or how many products already use it, and it'll be much more convincing.

lines.speaker: tom
lines.text: Last one is the bit about glass bottles.

lines.speaker: lang
lines.text: To be honest, that wasn't really about food packaging at all. It was mainly about drinks and recycling. I'd take it out altogether.

lines.speaker: rosa
lines.text: That's really useful. Thank you.

units.title: Test 2 · Part 4: How Desert Plants Survive
units.goal: Questions 31–40: note completion, ONE WORD ONLY, from a biology lecture; follow the three parts of the talk.

blocks.text: You will hear part of a lecture. Read the notes first. In Part 4 there is no pause in the middle, and the recording plays once.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Part four. You will hear a lecture on how desert plants survive with very little water. First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.

lines.speaker: lect
lines.text: Good morning, everyone. In today's lecture I want to look at one of the toughest problems in nature: how plants survive in deserts, where it may not rain for months, sometimes years. I'll look at three areas: roots, stems and leaves, and finally timing.

lines.speaker: lect
lines.text: First, though, a quick definition. When we say desert, we don't necessarily mean somewhere hot and sandy. Scientists usually define a desert as any place that gets less than about two hundred and fifty millimetres of rain a year. So parts of Antarctica count as desert too, although today I'll be talking about the hot ones.

lines.speaker: lect
lines.text: Let's start underground. Many desert plants have two quite different root systems. The first is a wide network of fine roots that spread out sideways, often several metres, just below the surface. When rain does come, it usually doesn't soak in very far, so these roots are there to catch it quickly before it evaporates.

lines.speaker: lect
lines.text: The second system goes in the opposite direction. Some shrubs send a single root straight down, sometimes more than fifty metres, until it reaches groundwater. This gives the plant a steady supply even in the driest years, although it takes a long time to grow.

lines.speaker: lect
lines.text: Now to the parts above ground. Cacti are the obvious example. Their stems store water, and many of them are covered in vertical folds. After rain, these folds open out, rather like an accordion, so the stem can swell and hold much more. In a dry period the stem slowly shrinks again.

lines.speaker: lect
lines.text: A large cactus can take in hundreds of litres after a single storm, and some of the biggest weigh several tonnes when they're full.

lines.speaker: lect
lines.text: What about the spines? People usually say they're there to stop animals eating the plant. That's partly true, but it isn't their main job. Thousands of spines together provide shade, and that keeps the surface of the stem cooler and reduces water loss.

lines.speaker: lect
lines.text: Plants that do have leaves tend to keep them small. And the leaves are often covered with a thin layer of wax. You can sometimes see it as a grey or shiny coating, and it works a bit like a raincoat in reverse: it keeps water in rather than out.

lines.speaker: lect
lines.text: Some shrubs go even further and simply drop their leaves when the dry season starts. They stand there looking bare and lifeless for months, but as soon as it rains, new leaves appear, sometimes within a few days. It's a bit like a tree in a northern winter, except the problem is drought rather than cold.

lines.speaker: lect
lines.text: Next, and this is the clever part, timing. Plants take in carbon dioxide through tiny holes called stomata, but every time the holes open, water escapes. Most plants open them during the day. Many desert plants, however, keep them shut in the heat and open them only at night, when it's cooler, and store the carbon dioxide until morning.

lines.speaker: lect
lines.text: This saves a huge amount of water, but there's a price. Plants that work this way have much slower growth than ordinary plants, which is one reason a cactus can take decades to reach full size.

lines.speaker: lect
lines.text: Timing matters for seeds too. In a dry year, many desert seeds don't germinate at all. It was once thought they could only survive for a few months like this, and later people said a few years. We now know that some can stay dormant for decades, waiting for one good rain.

lines.speaker: lect
lines.text: The most extreme case is the so-called resurrection plant. It can lose almost all of its water and look completely dead, brown and curled up. But give it water and it turns green again. People expect this to take days, but in fact it recovers within hours.

lines.speaker: lect
lines.text: Why does all this matter beyond the desert? As droughts become more common, scientists are studying the genes behind these features. The hope is to develop food crops that need less irrigation, which would make a real difference to farmers in dry regions.

lines.speaker: lect
lines.text: In the next session we'll look at desert animals. Thank you.

lines.text: That is the end of Part four.
